Radar cross section (RCS) reduction is critical for stealth target design.
Microwave absorbers coated on target surfaces are flexible, cost-effective, and widely used for RCS reduction.
The designed absorbers cover a frequency range from 2.0 to 18.0 GHz, matching most radar bands.
Two composite materials with 10% and 35% carbonyl iron powder (CIP) concentrations are used for matching and absorbing layers respectively.
Transmission Line Theory (TLT) models the multilayer absorber as a transmission line to calculate reflection coefficients.
Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) is used to optimize layer thicknesses and number of layers.
Seven multilayer designs (Type I to Type VII) were developed with varying layers and thicknesses.
Single-layer absorbers (Type I and II) have narrow bandwidth and poor absorption performance.
Type-IV design is a two-layer absorber with total thickness 3.0 mm and bandwidth nearly 15 GHz.
Type-VII design is a five-layer absorber with air gaps, total thickness 5.37 mm, and improved low-frequency absorption.
Both Type-IV and Type-VII designs are insensitive to incident wave angles up to 45° and to polarization.
Coating a PEC cylinder with Type-IV or Type-VII absorbers reduces RCS by at least 8 dB across most of 2.0 to 18.0 GHz.
Type-IV coating achieves up to 17.5 dB RCS reduction at 17 GHz; Type-VII achieves up to 16.5 dB at 12 GHz.
Increasing the number of layers and total thickness improves absorption performance and bandwidth.
The designed absorbers are very thin relative to radar wavelengths (e.g., 3 mm thickness vs. 60 mm cylinder radius).
Complex permittivity and permeability of composite materials are stable over the radar frequency range.
The absorbers maintain good performance on curved surfaces, not just planar infinite plates.
The method combining TLT and PSO simplifies design compared to full-wave EM simulations.
Metamaterial absorbers typically have narrow bandwidth and angle sensitivity, which the proposed composites overcome.
The absorbers have potential industrial applications due to their broadband, thin, and angle-insensitive properties.
